titre: Blood Vessels Found in a Tyrannosaurus rex Femur
accroche: In 2005, a paleontologist publishes the discovery of still-flexible blood vessels in a dinosaur femur 68 million years old.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 2000, John Horner's team discovers in Montana a skeleton of *Tyrannosaurus rex* (specimen MOR 1125). After about two years of excavation in the field, the femur is handed to the paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, of North Carolina State University, who sets out to dissolve its mineral in a weak acid: a common protocol for isolating what remains organic in a fossil bone. What she draws from it is anything but common: soft, transparent, branching structures that stretch and return to their shape under forceps, and that look uncannily like blood vessels.

## A Bone That Should No Longer Have Contained Anything Soft

The bone, 68 million years old, should no longer contain anything flexible: in paleontology, soft tissues are supposed to decompose in a few tens of thousands of years at most, gradually replaced by minerals. Schweitzer and her team publish their results in March 2005 in *Science*: the hollow vessels contain small round structures that look like cells, and the whole compares point by point to vessels extracted from the bone of a living ostrich. In 2007, a second team, led by John Asara, goes further: it sequences by mass spectrometry fragments of collagen preserved in this same bone. Of the seven sequences obtained, three come closest to those of chicken, the others to those of frog, newt or several species at once (the alligator, closer to the dinosaurs, is not yet in the comparison databases): a molecular clue pointing toward the kinship between dinosaurs and birds, where that kinship had until then rested only on the shape of bones.

## An Observation That Shifts a Doctrine

The discovery remains debated. In 2008, a team led by Thomas Kaye proposes a more conservative explanation: the observed structures would be recent bacterial biofilms, which would have molded the bone's cavities and, once the bone was dissolved in acid, taken on the appearance of vessels and cells. But comparable organic structures have since been found in fossils that were in no way exceptionally preserved: in 2015, a team led by Sergio Bertazzo reports fibers compatible with collagen and structures close to red blood cells in Cretaceous dinosaur bones 75 million years old. A preservation mechanism has also begun to take shape: in 2014, Schweitzer and her team show that iron released by hemoglobin, in an oxygen-poor environment, experimentally prolongs the preservation of ostrich blood vessels well beyond their normal lifespan. What this shifts is the idea that a fossil is an entirely mineralized object, in which nothing of the living remains but the shape.

repere.texte: The femur of specimen MOR 1125, 68 million years old, yielded flexible blood vessels and cellular structures in 2005; in 2007, the collagen fragments sequenced from it by mass spectrometry came closest to those of chicken.
repere.source: Schweitzer et al., “Soft-Tissue Vessels and Cellular Preservation in Tyrannosaurus rex,” Science, 2005

carte.punch: A Tyrannosaurus rex femur yielded still-flexible blood vessels in 2005.
carte.idee: Mary Schweitzer publishes in 2005 the discovery, in a Tyrannosaurus rex femur 68 million years old, of flexible vessels and cellular structures. In 2007, the collagen sequenced from it comes closest to that of chicken, a clue to the kinship between dinosaurs and birds.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Soft-Tissue Vessels and Cellular Preservation in Tyrannosaurus rex - Science
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The 2005 article, for the detail of the demineralization protocol.

quiz.question: What did the mass spectrometry sequencing of the collagen extracted from the Tyrannosaurus rex femur in 2007 reveal?
choix: That the collagen contained no usable trace, which closed the molecular lead
That the fragments corresponded mostly to alligator collagen, confirming kinship with living reptiles
That the dinosaur's complete DNA had been reconstructed from these fragments
That the collagen fragments came closest to those of chicken, among the species compared
quiz.explication: Of the seven collagen sequences obtained by Asara's team, three come closest to those of chicken among the organisms compared, a molecular clue pointing toward the kinship between dinosaurs and birds: it is not DNA, and the alligator, closer phylogenetically, was not yet in the comparison databases used in 2007.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What alternative hypothesis does Thomas Kaye's team propose in 2008 to explain the structures observed in the femur?
choix: That they are recent bacterial biofilms, which molded the bone's cavities after its demineralization
That they are perfectly preserved Tyrannosaurus DNA fragments
That they are calcite crystals formed during the animal's life
That they are remains of another animal that occupied the bone after the dinosaur's death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kaye and his team propose that the observed structures are recent bacterial biofilms that molded the bone's cavities, once it was dissolved in acid, rather than original fossil tissues.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Bertazzo and his team find in 2015 in Cretaceous dinosaur bones 75 million years old?
choix: A complete dinosaur skeleton never described before
Traces of complete DNA allowing the dinosaur's genome to be reconstructed
Probable collagen fibers and structures close to red blood cells, without exceptional preservation
Still-colored fossilized feathers, similar to those of living birds
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bertazzo and his team report fibers compatible with collagen and structures close to red blood cells in Cretaceous dinosaur bones that were in no way exceptionally preserved, extending the observation beyond the Tyrannosaurus femur alone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Mary Schweitzer's team show experimentally in 2014 about the preservation of soft tissues?
choix: That only bones immersed in fresh water can preserve soft tissues
That iron from hemoglobin, in an oxygen-poor environment, prolongs the preservation of ostrich vessels
That freezing is the only mechanism capable of explaining the preservation of ancient tissues
That soft tissues can be preserved only in amber, never in bone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Schweitzer and her team show that iron released by hemoglobin, combined with an oxygen-poor environment, experimentally prolongs the preservation of ostrich blood vessels well beyond their normal lifespan.
